programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
The final week of heats continues as another group of ambitious professional chefs steps up to prove they have the talent and technique to progress in the competition. But before they can look ahead, they must navigate two demanding challenges that will put their culinary skills and composure to the test.
First, it’s the skills test, where the chefs must fillet a sea bream and use it to create a shellfish risotto, finished with a spinach garnish. It’s a deceptively demanding dish, requiring sharp filleting skills to prepare the fish cleanly, precise timing to achieve perfectly cooked rice and the finesse to build a rich, balanced risotto without losing the delicate flavours of the seafood. Every element must come together seamlessly, with no room to hide behind elaborate presentation.
For some, the combination of intricate preparation and exacting technique proves daunting, leaving them struggling to keep pace. Others take the challenge in their stride, showing the confidence and control of seasoned professionals. Will the chefs’ efforts impress the judges, or will their shortcomings leave Marcus and Monica questioning whether they have what it takes to make it to the next stage?
With the skills test behind them, the chefs have the chance to show Marcus and Monica what they can do when given the freedom to cook their own food. In the signature dish round, they have 90 minutes to create a plate that reflects their personality, showcases their strengths and makes a compelling case for why they deserve to progress.

programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Glasgow - A Fix at the Top of the Cathedral ║ S1
programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Dom and Lucia are in Scotland’s biggest city for one of their biggest, or at least highest, fixes yet. Roof works mean once-in-a-generation access to Glasgow Cathedral’s weathervane, so the pair are helping blacksmith Stacey and apprentice Jameel clean and re-gild this iconic cockerel. The medieval building has a storied history, but it definitely predates lifts, so Lucia volunteers to go boldly where no Repair Shop expert has gone before – straight to the top of the 225-foot-high spire.
Back on solid ground, Kaming, a member of Glasgow’s Hakka Chinese community, has a Chinese unicorn head he hopes Lucia can bring back to life. The fragile bamboo-and-paper mask plays an important part in celebrations and festivities, but years of vigorous dancing have left it tattered and torn, its once-proud horn now held on with sticky tape. As he is the last person, as far as he is aware, who still knows how to do the traditional dance associated with the mask, he hopes having the costume repaired will mean he’s able to teach it to future generations before it's lost forever. It’s not a simple fix though, as Lucia has to contend with unfamiliar materials and balance her artistic restoration with creating a mask that will stand up structurally to years' more use in the future.
As they travel the country, the Repair Shop experts love to meet fellow craftspeople, but it’s not all stonemasonry and pottery. There’s been a vibrant graffiti scene in Glasgow for decades, and Dom is meeting celebrated street artist Pizzaboy to discover how his large-scale works engage with the local community. programme.desc:
Five chefs remain in the race for a spot in the quarter-final, but first they must impress in two more challenges designed to test their creativity, precision and technical ability.
Marcus and Monica are joined by acclaimed South African chef Ash Valenzuela-Heeger, winner of the prestigious 2025 Michelin Young Chef Award. Her impressive career has seen her hone her craft at some of the world’s most celebrated restaurants, including London’s three-Michelin-starred Ledbury and Cape Town’s renowned Test Kitchen. She has since made her mark with Riverine Rabbit in Birmingham, which earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand in 2025.
Known for her bold, inventive cooking, Ash draws on her South African heritage and international influences, with live-fire techniques at the heart of her culinary style. She challenges the chefs to cook BBQ beef sirloin, served with BBQ maitake mushrooms, caramelised roscoff onions and a cafe au lait sauce. It’s a brief that demands a sophisticated understanding of flavour, smoke and fire, and the ability to make every element work in harmony.
With the standard rising and a quarter-final place within reach, can the contestants deliver a plate worthy of this award-winning chef’s exacting standards?
The signature dessert round is the final hurdle, and the chefs must show that they have the range and imagination to compete with the very best. This is their chance to take risks, bring their own ideas to the plate and prove that they can deliver something truly memorable. But sweet cooking demands a different kind of judgement; flavours must work in harmony, textures need to complement one another, and the finishing touches can make all the difference between a good dessert and a great one.
Marcus and Monica have seen what the chefs can do with savoury ingredients, but now they must decide who has the finesse and creative flair to progress to the next stage of the competition. As the final plates are tasted, will the desserts be enough to secure a place in the quarter-final? And whose MasterChef journey must come to an end? First up is the invention test, and the secret ingredient has a history stretching back more than 2,000 years: miso. A staple of Japanese cuisine, this fermented paste brings extraordinary depth, savoury complexity and umami to a dish. With different varieties offering their own distinctive flavours, the chefs must work out how best to make miso the star of the plate. programme.title: Bargain Hunt
programme.desc:
Antiques meet archaeology in this episode from West Sussex. In the village of Fishbourne, Natasha Raskin Sharp learns about the discovery of a huge Roman palace by workmen in the 1960s. In the company of curator Dr Rob Symmons, she hears how part of the palace and its treasures were unearthed over eight summers by hundreds of volunteers. One of the highlights is an exquisite mosaic featuring mythical sea creatures around which the owner – a high-ranking Roman – and his guests would have sat to eat meals. Another highlight is a partially smashed statue of Emperor Nero and a remarkably rare rabbit bone.
Hoping to unearth their own treasures are two teams of bargain hunters at Ardingly antiques fair. In blue are cousins Michelle and Emma, and in red are golfing pals Linda and Yvonne. With expert Caroline Hawley by their side, the reds get off to an explosive start, eyeing up a pair of powder flasks. Meanwhile, Emma spots a West German pottery vase, but expert Thomas Forrester doubts that profits will bloom at auction.

programme.title: The Northumbria Mysteries
programme.desc:
When a burnt-out delivery van is discovered on a quiet rural road, Rose and Raj are met with a grim crime scene: a charred body in the passenger seat and no sign of the driver. Sifting through the ashes, they uncover a bizarre assortment of clues, including a melted key fob, rusted gardening tools and a bottle of imported Polish vodka.
Tracking down the van’s insured drivers leads them to Kelly Prudham, a tight-lipped agency cleaner, and Scott Smith, a devoted widowed father missing since the previous evening. Is Scott the vanished driver, or is he the unidentified victim in the passenger seat? Kelly claims concern for Scott’s young daughter Chloe, yet she stonewalls every question. However, Rose’s sharp eyes spot an identical bottle of Polish vodka in Kelly’s flat, indicating that Kelly may have a dangerous motive for concealing her and Scott’s recent movements.
Meanwhile, Joe can’t resist probing into the mystery. Dragging Brother Christopher along, he snoops around the crime scene and dives into Scott’s past. Relying on his sharp human intuition and feeling somewhat aligned with this man who seems to be struggling as a father, Joe forms a bold theory about Scott’s whereabouts. But his covert search goes sideways, stranding Joe and Christopher in a perilous predicament deep in the Northumbrian moors.
With time running out and danger escalating, Rose, Joe and Raj must pool their findings to identify the burnt remains, track down the arsonist and expose the motive behind the blaze before the truth burns out completely. programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: East Lothian - Saving the Musselburgh Carriage ║ S1
programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Kirsten are in Musselburgh, on Scotland’s east coast. It’s a town boasting a proud heritage that is celebrated each year with a procession led by their elected Honest Lad and Honest Lass. However, for the past few years, the antique carriage these local luminaries ride in has been off the road. Restoring the carriage is a huge job that requires the skills of local signwriter Ross Hastie and wheelwright Greg Rowland, and made more complicated by the impending deadline of this year’s festival.
It's a bit of a musical mystery when the team are faced with Erica’s Stroviol. In the family since the 1930s, it belonged to Erica's father, who was a passionate musician who played in several local groups. The distinctive horn has become detached from this turn-of-the-century musical oddity, so it might take more than just the skills of stringed instrument expert Becky Houghton to get a tune out of it once again.
In nearby Edinburgh, Will stops off at Stewart Christie & Co, Scotland’s oldest bespoke tailors, to discover how their handmade tweed clothes balance modern demands with century-old techniques. Will gets an insight into every step of the process, from an initial measuring to getting on the scissors himself and cutting out his own waistcoat pattern from the tweed cloth the company built their name on. programme.title: Policing Paradise
programme.desc:
With exclusive access to the police service on the paradise island of Bermuda, we follow life on the front line for the near 400 officers keeping both holidaymakers and locals safe. From patrols and traffic operations to the drug unit, forensics, tactical response teams, the coastguard and community policing, the series goes behind the scenes with the officers at the heart of the action.
The island has its fair share of challenges on both land and sea, with more than 3,000 crimes committed each year. We show how these dedicated officers, including around 30 from the UK, deal with the highs and lows of policing this British Overseas Territory.
In the centre of the island, Sergeant Milton Hill responds to reports of an elderly man walking along a busy roadside in clear distress. When he arrives, the man is unable to recall his name, address or basic personal details, and the mystery begins. Concerned for his safety, Milton stays close, guiding traffic around him as he repeatedly steps into the road. On an island where everyone knows everyone, Officer Milton sends a photograph of the man to base, where his identity provides a surprising twist to the tale. It's a race against time for Officer Milton to get him returned home safely.
Elsewhere, PC Eddie Smith and PC Jameela Sabir are on a stop-and-search operation. When Sergeant Mervin Homer examines a bike, he discovers a dangerous switchblade hidden under the seat. With the rider offering no feasible explanation, the prohibited weapon is immediately seized. Back at Hamilton Police Station, Custody Sergeant Francis Blackman reads the bike rider their rights, while Assistant Commissioner Martin Weekes examines other recently confiscated blades, including machetes and a samurai sword.
At Bermuda’s international airport, PC Paul 'Geordie' Watson supports Customs Officer Malcolm Martin and drugs dog Zorro while screening an incoming flight from Canada. After sweeping the aircraft cabin in just five minutes, Zorro indicates interest in two bags in the arrivals hall, leaving customs officers the job of discreetly monitoring the family before searching their bags and bringing them in for questioning. What will the canine team uncover next?

programme.title: Celebration Kitchen
programme.desc:
Matt Tebbutt hosts this special edition celebrating Guru Nanak Gurpurab or the Birthday of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. Considered one of the most important Sikh holy days, it is a revered celebration in Sikhism which brings people together in devotion, reflection and unity.
Every year, the occasion is marked on the full moon day of the Kartik month, which is also known as Kartik Purnima, and falls on Tuesday 24 November this year. Three exceptional cooks join Matt in the studio to share their delicious recipes that are perfect for the celebration. Award-winning British Indian food writer, columnist and trend consultant Gurdeep Loyal prepares extra-crispy potato and chickpea tikkis with a tamarind and date chutney, which would traditionally be served as street food outside the temple. Food writer, restaurateur and chef-owner of Jikoni, Ravinder Bhogal, prepares a decadent, celebratory vegetarian platter, and as no feast is complete without a sweet treat, Manpreet Singh Ahuja, aka the Singing Chef, serves up a trio of delicious sweets, including the pinnis that he remembers his mother and grandmother making for Guru Nanak Ji's birthday.
Celebrity guests include doctor and BAFTA award-winning TV presenter Dr Ranj Singh, journalist, broadcaster and best-selling author Sathnam Sanghera and journalist, broadcaster and Good Morning Britain host Ranvir Singh, who shares her cherished Guru Nanak Gurpurab traditions, memories and food favourites from the celebration. The programme also features highlights from the BBC archives. It is a show filled with fun, food and fascinating insights into one of the most important days in the Sikh calendar. programme.title: Songs of Praise
programme.desc:
Sean Fletcher is in Liverpool to meet celebrated screenwriter, author and former Children’s Laureate Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who chooses his favourite hymns and reflects on life, faith and the value of wonder.
Sean meets Frank at Liverpool’s historic waterfront, where Frank's story began, and discovers how a childhood steeped in Catholic community and the stories of saints inspired his young imagination.
In Liverpool’s Central Library, Sean hears how Frank went on to become a screenwriter for TV and film, and a best-selling children’s author. He also reveals how he came to write the narrative for the iconic opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics and why the concept of wonder has always been crucial to his work and faith.
Their journey through Liverpool finally brings them to the city’s iconic Metropolitan Cathedral, where Frank talks of the architecture as a prayer and tells of hearing his children sing there many years ago.

programme.desc:
The oceans have seasons just as the land does. Stretching across the temperate bands located between the freezing poles and the warm tropics lie the seasonal seas. Life is tough in these constantly changing waters, but if animals can persevere and adapt to change, there are myriad opportunities to not only survive but thrive here.
Winter in the seasonal seas is a battlefield. Storms whip up immense waves that can travel for thousands of miles, building to 30 metres in height before making landfall. On the Pacific coast of South America, such waves impact the lives of South America sea lions that have lived on this exposed coast for generations. Newborn pups and mothers are restricted to the colony, but the most intrepid males take a risk, leaving the tempestuous coast for unfamiliar waters and unusual prey - black-necked swans.
Some choose to escape, whilst others are undeterred by winters icy grip on the seasonal seas. In Patagonia, a female southern right whale arrives in the protected bay where she was likely born, in search of a mate. Testing prospective partners before accepting the best mate, she is rewarded with a gentle belly rub and embrace - a valuable pairing given that these animals were hunted to near extinction in the last century. The whaling ban increased this population from just 300 to 25,000, with a surprising twist – white calves.
As daylight lengthens and spring approaches, the greening of the seasonal seas commences. Plankton multiplies, creating huge blooms and feeding many species, including a rather peculiar crustacean, a porcelain crab. In the waters off Chile, over 200 million feast on this bounty, forming the largest-known aggregation of crabs in our oceans. But with limited space and an increased flow of plankton, the crabs do something remarkable - they organise themselves into structured lines, a behaviour that has never been filmed before.
As forests flourish on land, they also do so in the water. In spring, kelp, one of the fastest-growing organisms on earth, can lengthen by half a metre a day, forming submarine jungles that are home to a variety of creatures. In Japan, these lush fronds conceal a rarely seen fish, an eelpout, with a length of just ten centimetres.

programme.desc:
The roadshow comes from Alexandra Gardens in the heart of Cardiff, where treasures include a Maori pipe, a book listing wartime spies and a rare SAS medal collection.
Ronnie Archer-Morgan is thrilled to see a pipe by a renowned Maori craftsman, whilst Geoffrey Munn is dazzled by a jewel-encrusted stick pin given as a gift from King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra.
There are plenty of Welsh treasures to be found, including an autograph book featuring a Tom Jones signature and early concert ticket, and Lisa Lloyd challenges Fiona to spot the most valuable item in a group of three pieces of rare rugby memorabilia.
Marc Allum is stunned to see a remarkable archive of First World War-era photographs documenting arrivals into Cardiff Docks, some of whom were suspected of being spies, and militaria expert Mark Smith is humbled by a group of medals and a cap badge belonging to one of the earliest members of the SAS.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
In the frozen waters of the Arctic, a bowhead whale breaks the sea ice with its skull to breathe - completely at home in this seemingly hostile sea. Polar waters may seem remote, but their influence supports more than the wildlife that thrives there by helping to power a global system of ocean currents that creates extraordinary opportunities for wildlife far beyond the ice.
In the Falkland Islands, nutrient-rich water flowing north from Antarctica sustains a colony of king penguins. But returning parents weighed down with food for their chicks must try to cross a beach patrolled by an extraordinary southern sea lion, the only one known to regularly hunt king penguins on land.
Cold water from the Arctic also travels thousands of miles. In the Pacific, it cools the coast of Japan, where a male dwarf lumpsucker, about the size of a pea, must find a nest and persuade a female to enter. Once she has laid her eggs, he becomes a devoted single father, guarding them from hungry predators for 40 days and nights.
Around Antarctica, hundreds of fin whales converge on one of the greatest feeding grounds on earth. They work together in a spectacular synchronised formation, turning clockwise before lunging onto their sides to feast on Antarctic krill. Beneath the continent’s sea ice lies a remarkable world where giant sea spiders clamber over ancient glass sponges and a tiny amphipod escapes hungry icefish by hitching a ride on sea angels and venomous jellyfish.
The influence of the polar waters is so strong that it helps power global currents that cross entire oceans and circle the planet. In the North Atlantic, the Gulf Stream brings warm water from the Caribbean to the shores of Britain, attracting Atlantic bluefin tuna to hunt off the Cornish coast. These powerful predators, which can attack at 45 miles per hour, have only recently returned to British shores following international action to protect them.
But the currents all these animals rely on are changing. With a loss of sea ice, many are now weakening, driving animals to adapt – sometimes in surprising ways. Around Newfoundland, green sea urchins are losing the kelp forests that once protected them from the sun’s ultraviolet rays.

However, between Michael’s mechanical know-how and Will’s paintwork, the train might just be brought back into service.

She is in Corsock to learn the secrets behind slipware from potters Doug and Hannah, who are preserving this medieval technique, which uses liquid clay known as slip to decorate pots, jugs and anything else for the home. However, it’s a messy business, so Kirsten’s white jacket may not make it through unscathed. There’s a lot changing for Stacey and Joe as they discover they’ve found a buyer for Pickle Cottage and take another step towards moving house. But before they can think too much about packing boxes, there’s plenty to keep them busy – including getting the lake ready for its newest residents.

programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
The final week of heats continues as another group of ambitious professional chefs steps up to prove they have the talent and technique to progress in the competition. But before they can look ahead, they must navigate two demanding challenges that will put their culinary skills and composure to the test.
First, it’s the skills test, where the chefs must fillet a sea bream and use it to create a shellfish risotto, finished with a spinach garnish. It’s a deceptively demanding dish, requiring sharp filleting skills to prepare the fish cleanly, precise timing to achieve perfectly cooked rice and the finesse to build a rich, balanced risotto without losing the delicate flavours of the seafood. Every element must come together seamlessly, with no room to hide behind elaborate presentation.
For some, the combination of intricate preparation and exacting technique proves daunting, leaving them struggling to keep pace. Others take the challenge in their stride, showing the confidence and control of seasoned professionals. Will the chefs’ efforts impress the judges, or will their shortcomings leave Marcus and Monica questioning whether they have what it takes to make it to the next stage?
With the skills test behind them, the chefs have the chance to show Marcus and Monica what they can do when given the freedom to cook their own food. In the signature dish round, they have 90 minutes to create a plate that reflects their personality, showcases their strengths and makes a compelling case for why they deserve to progress.
For some, it’s an opportunity to demonstrate real ambition and push their cooking in exciting new directions. For others, finding the right balance between ambition and execution proves more difficult.
The judges must decide whose cooking has made a strong enough impression to keep them in the running and whose journey ends here. programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Glasgow - A Fix at the Top of the Cathedral ║ S1
programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Dom and Lucia are in Scotland’s biggest city for one of their biggest, or at least highest, fixes yet. Roof works mean once-in-a-generation access to Glasgow Cathedral’s weathervane, so the pair are helping blacksmith Stacey and apprentice Jameel clean and re-gild this iconic cockerel. The medieval building has a storied history, but it definitely predates lifts, so Lucia volunteers to go boldly where no Repair Shop expert has gone before – straight to the top of the 225-foot-high spire.
Back on solid ground, Kaming, a member of Glasgow’s Hakka Chinese community, has a Chinese unicorn head he hopes Lucia can bring back to life. The fragile bamboo-and-paper mask plays an important part in celebrations and festivities, but years of vigorous dancing have left it tattered and torn, its once-proud horn now held on with sticky tape. As he is the last person, as far as he is aware, who still knows how to do the traditional dance associated with the mask, he hopes having the costume repaired will mean he’s able to teach it to future generations before it's lost forever. It’s not a simple fix though, as Lucia has to contend with unfamiliar materials and balance her artistic restoration with creating a mask that will stand up structurally to years' more use in the future.
As they travel the country, the Repair Shop experts love to meet fellow craftspeople, but it’s not all stonemasonry and pottery. There’s been a vibrant graffiti scene in Glasgow for decades, and Dom is meeting celebrated street artist Pizzaboy to discover how his large-scale works engage with the local community. programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
Five chefs remain in the race for a spot in the quarter-final, but first they must impress in two more challenges designed to test their creativity, precision and technical ability.
Marcus and Monica are joined by acclaimed South African chef Ash Valenzuela-Heeger, winner of the prestigious 2025 Michelin Young Chef Award. Her impressive career has seen her hone her craft at some of the world’s most celebrated restaurants, including London’s three-Michelin-starred Ledbury and Cape Town’s renowned Test Kitchen. She has since made her mark with Riverine Rabbit in Birmingham, which earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand in 2025.
Known for her bold, inventive cooking, Ash draws on her South African heritage and international influences, with live-fire techniques at the heart of her culinary style. She challenges the chefs to cook BBQ beef sirloin, served with BBQ maitake mushrooms, caramelised roscoff onions and a cafe au lait sauce. It’s a brief that demands a sophisticated understanding of flavour, smoke and fire, and the ability to make every element work in harmony.
With the standard rising and a quarter-final place within reach, can the contestants deliver a plate worthy of this award-winning chef’s exacting standards?
The signature dessert round is the final hurdle, and the chefs must show that they have the range and imagination to compete with the very best. This is their chance to take risks, bring their own ideas to the plate and prove that they can deliver something truly memorable. But sweet cooking demands a different kind of judgement; flavours must work in harmony, textures need to complement one another, and the finishing touches can make all the difference between a good dessert and a great one.
Marcus and Monica have seen what the chefs can do with savoury ingredients, but now they must decide who has the finesse and creative flair to progress to the next stage of the competition. As the final plates are tasted, will the desserts be enough to secure a place in the quarter-final? And whose MasterChef journey must come to an end? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
It’s the last quarter-final of the series, and with a place in knockout week at stake, there’s everything to play for. Four chefs return to the kitchen knowing that one false move could bring their ambitions to an abrupt end. Marcus and Monica are looking for the consistency, ingenuity and confidence that mark out a truly exceptional chef.
First up is the invention test, and the secret ingredient has a history stretching back more than 2,000 years: miso. A staple of Japanese cuisine, this fermented paste brings extraordinary depth, savoury complexity and umami to a dish. With different varieties offering their own distinctive flavours, the chefs must work out how best to make miso the star of the plate. Who will turn this humble ingredient into something exceptional, and who will fall short of expectations?
Then they face one last chance to prove they have what it takes to go all the way.
Three highly respected food writers and critics, Tom Parker Bowles, Leyla Kazim and Jimi Famurewa, wait to put the chefs’ cooking under the microscope. Between them, they’ve eaten at restaurants around the world and very little escapes their attention. They know what exceptional food looks, tastes and feels like, and they’ll be looking beyond technical skill to the details that separate a good meal from a truly memorable one.
The chefs must serve up a two-course menu that captures their culinary identity, showcases their abilities and gives these exacting critics something to talk about. Every choice matters, from the balance of flavours to the smallest finishing touch. Can they cook with enough originality and precision to make a lasting impression?
Back in the kitchen, Marcus and Monica face their biggest decision yet. With the quarter-finals coming to a close and only three places in knockout week up for grabs, they must consider the chefs’ performances across the challenges before deciding who has done enough to progress to the next stage. For those who fall short, there will be no second chance.
Who will take the next step towards the coveted MasterChef: The Professionals title, and whose journey ends at the final hurdle?

programme.title: Bargain Hunt
programme.desc:
Antiques meet archaeology in this episode from West Sussex. In the village of Fishbourne, Natasha Raskin Sharp learns about the discovery of a huge Roman palace by workmen in the 1960s. In the company of curator Dr Rob Symmons, she hears how part of the palace and its treasures were unearthed over eight summers by hundreds of volunteers. One of the highlights is an exquisite mosaic featuring mythical sea creatures around which the owner – a high-ranking Roman – and his guests would have sat to eat meals. Another highlight is a partially smashed statue of Emperor Nero and a remarkably rare rabbit bone.
Hoping to unearth their own treasures are two teams of bargain hunters at Ardingly antiques fair. In blue are cousins Michelle and Emma, and in red are golfing pals Linda and Yvonne. With expert Caroline Hawley by their side, the reds get off to an explosive start, eyeing up a pair of powder flasks. programme.title: The Northumbria Mysteries
programme.desc:
When a burnt-out delivery van is discovered on a quiet rural road, Rose and Raj are met with a grim crime scene: a charred body in the passenger seat and no sign of the driver. Sifting through the ashes, they uncover a bizarre assortment of clues, including a melted key fob, rusted gardening tools and a bottle of imported Polish vodka.
Tracking down the van’s insured drivers leads them to Kelly Prudham, a tight-lipped agency cleaner, and Scott Smith, a devoted widowed father missing since the previous evening. Is Scott the vanished driver, or is he the unidentified victim in the passenger seat? Kelly claims concern for Scott’s young daughter Chloe, yet she stonewalls every question. However, Rose’s sharp eyes spot an identical bottle of Polish vodka in Kelly’s flat, indicating that Kelly may have a dangerous motive for concealing her and Scott’s recent movements.
Meanwhile, Joe can’t resist probing into the mystery. Dragging Brother Christopher along, he snoops around the crime scene and dives into Scott’s past. Relying on his sharp human intuition and feeling somewhat aligned with this man who seems to be struggling as a father, Joe forms a bold theory about Scott’s whereabouts. But his covert search goes sideways, stranding Joe and Christopher in a perilous predicament deep in the Northumbrian moors.
With time running out and danger escalating, Rose, Joe and Raj must pool their findings to identify the burnt remains, track down the arsonist and expose the motive behind the blaze before the truth burns out completely. programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: East Lothian - Saving the Musselburgh Carriage ║ S1
programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Kirsten are in Musselburgh, on Scotland’s east coast. It’s a town boasting a proud heritage that is celebrated each year with a procession led by their elected Honest Lad and Honest Lass. However, for the past few years, the antique carriage these local luminaries ride in has been off the road. Restoring the carriage is a huge job that requires the skills of local signwriter Ross Hastie and wheelwright Greg Rowland, and made more complicated by the impending deadline of this year’s festival.
It's a bit of a musical mystery when the team are faced with Erica’s Stroviol. In the family since the 1930s, it belonged to Erica's father, who was a passionate musician who played in several local groups. The distinctive horn has become detached from this turn-of-the-century musical oddity, so it might take more than just the skills of stringed instrument expert Becky Houghton to get a tune out of it once again.
In nearby Edinburgh, Will stops off at Stewart Christie & Co, Scotland’s oldest bespoke tailors, to discover how their handmade tweed clothes balance modern demands with century-old techniques. Will gets an insight into every step of the process, from an initial measuring to getting on the scissors himself and cutting out his own waistcoat pattern from the tweed cloth the company built their name on. programme.title: Bargain Hunt
programme.desc:
Eric Knowles visits Nottingham’s Gothic revival cathedral to learn how conservators are revealing 19th-century artwork under decades of plaster and paint. Designed in 1842 by architect Augustus Pugin, the cathedral’s interior was whitewashed in the 1960s. Pugin is widely admired for his work on some of Britain’s most famous buildings, including the Palace of Westminster. Conservator Ana Logreira shows Eric how they are using digitally created stencils to renovate the cathedral’s historic interior.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
In the frozen waters of the Arctic, a bowhead whale breaks the sea ice with its skull to breathe - completely at home in this seemingly hostile sea. Polar waters may seem remote, but their influence supports more than the wildlife that thrives there by helping to power a global system of ocean currents that creates extraordinary opportunities for wildlife far beyond the ice.
In the Falkland Islands, nutrient-rich water flowing north from Antarctica sustains a colony of king penguins. But returning parents weighed down with food for their chicks must try to cross a beach patrolled by an extraordinary southern sea lion, the only one known to regularly hunt king penguins on land.
Cold water from the Arctic also travels thousands of miles. In the Pacific, it cools the coast of Japan, where a male dwarf lumpsucker, about the size of a pea, must find a nest and persuade a female to enter. Once she has laid her eggs, he becomes a devoted single father, guarding them from hungry predators for 40 days and nights.
Around Antarctica, hundreds of fin whales converge on one of the greatest feeding grounds on earth. They work together in a spectacular synchronised formation, turning clockwise before lunging onto their sides to feast on Antarctic krill. Beneath the continent’s sea ice lies a remarkable world where giant sea spiders clamber over ancient glass sponges and a tiny amphipod escapes hungry icefish by hitching a ride on sea angels and venomous jellyfish.
The influence of the polar waters is so strong that it helps power global currents that cross entire oceans and circle the planet. In the North Atlantic, the Gulf Stream brings warm water from the Caribbean to the shores of Britain, attracting Atlantic bluefin tuna to hunt off the Cornish coast. These powerful predators, which can attack at 45 miles per hour, have only recently returned to British shores following international action to protect them.
But the currents all these animals rely on are changing. With a loss of sea ice, many are now weakening, driving animals to adapt – sometimes in surprising ways. Around Newfoundland, green sea urchins are losing the kelp forests that once protected them from the sun’s ultraviolet rays.

programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
The stunning coastline of Northumberland is the setting for Michael Portillo’s rail adventure from the city of Newcastle to England’s northernmost town, Berwick-upon-Tweed. Travelling aboard the metro, the East Coast Main Line and the Tyne Valley line, Michael marvels at the scenery and admires the architectural and engineering legacy of the railways in the region where they were invented.
His route takes in the River Tyne, Hadrian’s Wall, a former mining village and the fishing port of Amble. Along the way, Michael visits Bamburgh Castle and the holy island of Lindisfarne.
In Tynemouth, Michael discovers one of the most treacherous coastlines in Britain and hears of a 19th-century tragedy at sea that inspired 140 local men to set up a coastal rescue service. The Tynemouth Volunteer Life Brigade trained rescuers to operate an ingenious apparatus called a breeches buoy from the shore. Michael finds out how it works and enjoys a pint and a sea shanty with long-serving volunteers.
At Long Sands beach, Michael rolls up his sleeves to help volunteers caring for sick and injured seals at the Tynemouth Aquarium Seal Hospital. A young pup called Gandalf needs to have his temperature taken.
From Newcastle Central, Michael boards The Passage to India train service, a curry express, which takes him 20 miles along the Tyne Valley line to the station house at Corbridge, now an Indian restaurant.
Back on the Tyne Valley line, Michael's train traces the course of the mighty Hadrian’s Wall. At Bardon Mill, he discovers some of the richest Roman archaeological sites in Britain at Vindolanda. Michael joins volunteer excavators to hear about some of their intriguing finds. programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
Michael Portillo continues his rail journey exploring England’s north east coast. Heading north from Newcastle, Michael discovers one of the city’s trendiest hotspots, Ouseburn, and is intrigued to hear of its part in Newcastle’s early industrial development.
En route, Michael travels through the huge Northumberland coalfield. At Cramlington, he alights to visit an extraordinary work of landform art made from the spoil of a coalmine, the vast Northumberlandia, known as the Lady of the North.
Next stop is the former coal port of Blyth. On the historic quayside Michael enjoys a hearty sea shanty and learns about an intrepid former townsman, Captain William Smith, who in 1819 discovered the Antarctic. Michael meets a group of young people who have been inspired by the captain’s story to restore a Scottish Herring drifter, called a Zulu, with the Blyth Tall Ships Charity.
At Bedlington, Michael hunts down a lost railway, whose services began in 1850 but closed to passengers in 1964 following the Beeching Report. The 18-mile coastal Blyth and Tyne Railway is however rising from the ashes and test trains are already on the track.
Lynemouth Power Station once used coal to produce electricity but today has switched to biomass. Michael boards a half-kilometre long freight train loaded with wood pellets bound for the power station. He hears from the train driver and the fuel manager at Lynemouth how the decline of coal has affected their working lives and the region in which they live, and he learns how rail is playing its part in saving carbon. programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
Michael Portillo explores the wild and rugged coastline of Northumberland by rail. He begins today in Morpeth, where he finds a historic collection of Northumbrian bagpipes and discovers how difficult they are to play.
The East Coast Main Line delivers Michael to Widdrington and its long sandy bay, where a beachcombing blacksmith finds treasures to inspire artwork in steel. Michael helps to put the finishing touches on a metal seaweed design.
At Rothbury, Michael visits Britain’s first smart home: a gadget-filled Victorian mansion built by wealthy industrialist and inventor, William Armstrong. Cragside clings to the side of a mountain and is full of such 19th-century mod cons as an early dishwasher, a water-powered roasting spit, central heating and hydroelectricity.
Heading back to the sea, Michael reaches the mouth of the River Coquet and the fishing port of Amble, home to one of the largest fleets of inshore fishing boats on this coast. In Central America, the crystal-clear waters of the Caribbean Sea meet jungle landscapes that support an extraordinary array of wildlife. It’s a perfect habitat that houses the highest density of some of the world’s most endangered animals.
In Belize, Liz goes on the trail of a jaguar that's suspected of stealing local pigs, joins local scientists in a high-adrenaline expedition to tag Antillean manatees, and meets the inspirational women who have increased the population of Yucatan black howler monkeys by ten times.
Travelling on to Costa Rica, Liz meets a man who took an enormous risk by turning his father’s farm into a haven for frogs, encounters a remarkable woman ensuring that the local wildlife thrives as her hometown grows, and discovers how to rehabilitate sloths, helping two of them to return to the wild. programme.title: The Repair Shop
programme.desc:
First into the barn, Gwyneth from Powys entrusts painting conservator Lucia with a remarkable but badly bruised portrait of her heroic ancestor Captain William Marshall, who risked his life to rescue over 100 shipwrecked Irish emigrants left stranded on an iceberg. The portrait was the precious possession of her late son Paul, who bore an extraordinary resemblance to his six-times great-grandfather, but the ravages of time have left it bent and buckled, with key elements, including the captain’s handsome features, obscured beneath yellowing varnish. After hours of painstaking repair work, Lucia welcomes Gwyneth back to the barn, on what would have been Paul’s birthday, to reveal the extraordinary results of her restoration.
Next, woodworker Will, bookbinder Chris and textiles conservator Rebecca join forces to rescue a well-travelled Jamaican trunk, otherwise known as a grip, that has seen far better days. Brought into the barn by Raphaelia Finlayson, the grip accompanied her father Aubrey, a singer, songwriter and record producer, all over the world as he travelled between Jamaica, London and the USA in pursuit of his musical dreams. Towards the end of Aubrey’s life, the battered wooden case held the vinyl records, sheet music and memorabilia of a lifetime spent in music, but now, damaged by decades of travel and storage, its wood is warped, its fabric is torn, and its paper lining has disintegrated. Will, Chris and Rebecca are determined to return the grip to its former glory, allowing Raphaelia to preserve her father’s mini museum and the legacy of his creative journey.
From Perth in Scotland, Andy brings a shattered plaster bust that for 20 years held pride of place in the family home he shared with his late wife, Diane. The bust originally caught the couple’s eye at a car boot sale because Andy felt it looked just like Diane, and it had sat proudly in their hallway ever since. However, an unfortunate accident saw it smashed to pieces, and ceramics restorer Kirsten Ramsay now faces the ultimate 3D jigsaw. Can she reassemble hundreds of fragments of plaster and bring the features so reminiscent of Diane back to life?

programme.title: Murder Case
programme.desc:
January 2017. Police continue their investigation into the murder of 23-year-old Cameron Logan, who died in a fire at his family home in Milngavie, near Glasgow. Bex Williams has suffered severe injuries in the fire that killed her boyfriend, but at last she is well enough to provide police with vital information about what happened on New Year’s Day. From her hospital bed, she recalls the horror of what she saw and heard during the attack, but she is unable to identify the masked intruder.
With the murderer still at large, detectives must look elsewhere for answers. Their attention turns to Cameron’s older brother Blair, and they discover the brothers had not always seen eye to eye. But could a family fall out really have led to such violent and deadly consequences? Blair tells police he was out jogging on the morning of the fire, and only returned when the emergency services were arriving. Could his absence simply be a coincidence, or is there more to his movements that morning?
Working alongside their forensic colleagues, detectives revisit the house, and they finally find a key piece of evidence that enables them to name a suspect. Bex begins the long process of recovery and grief, and speaking in a documentary for the first time, she details how she worked through the physical and emotional impact of the fire. With so much against her, Bex shows extraordinary strength and is determined to find justice for Cameron. Series Producer - Kirsty MacFarlane Production Manager - Eilidh Hart.

programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
Michael Portillo travels the length of the magnificent Northumbrian coastline with its glorious beaches and grandiose castles.
In the village of Alnmouth, he takes to the waves in a traditional skiff built by dedicated members of the Alnmouth Coastal Rowing Club. They’re training to compete in the World Championships in a boat based on a design from Fair Isle. Michael has to learn fast to stay afloat.
The Aln Valley heritage railway conveys Michael to Alnwick, crossing a 170-year-old viaduct built by Robert Stephenson. From the historic cobbled town with its imposing castle, Michael heads for the beach at Boulmer to hear about threats to this low-lying coastline and efforts to protect it from sea erosion and tidal surges.
Next stop for Michael is Chathill, which serves the 19th-century port of Seahouses, from which boats depart for the Farne Islands. Along this rocky coastline, Michael heads for the Olde Ship Inn to discover a fascinating map which charts the wrecks of many ships.
The mighty Bamburgh Castle, icon of Northumberland, is Michael’s last destination today. Once the seat of Northumbrian kings, the castle building was begun by the Normans, and since the late 19th century, has been in the hands of the Armstrong family. Michael meets the castle’s current keeper to hear about its history and admire its magnificent King’s Hall. Presenter - Michael Portillo Director - Beatrice Ni Bhroin Series Editor - Alison Kreps Executive Producer - John Comerford Production Company - Fremantle.

programme.title: Liz Bonnin's Wild Caribbean
programme.desc:
The volcanic islands of the Lesser Antilles, built by eruptions and shaped by the ocean surrounding them, are some of the most biodiverse landscapes of the Caribbean, where humans have developed a special relationship with their wild surroundings.
On Mayreau, Liz joins a team of residents repairing their vibrant coral, which has been damaged by disease. On neighbouring Union Island, she goes on patrol with a local environmental army to help protect the Union Island gecko, one of the smallest reptiles in the world.
In St Vincent, Liz hikes one of the most active volcanoes in the region – La Soufriere – to find the brightly coloured St Vincent parrot. And in her ancestral home of Trinidad, she relives one of her most magnificent wildlife encounters: the flight of the scarlet ibis. programme.title: Why...
programme.desc:
On 24th September 2025, the main road outside one of Bangkok's major hospitals collapsed. The giant sinkhole, the size of two tennis courts, snapped water pipes, ripped down power lines, and swallowed two vehicles.
During the day, it continued to grow, threatening the foundations of the hospital and forcing close to a thousand staff and patients to evacuate the building. Ampan Vimonvattana, vice dean of Vajira Hospital, witnessed the collapse: 'The earth swallowed everything... it pulled the road surface, the soil, anything on top. Even the electrical poles got dragged down. It was really scary.'
Why Sinkholes Collapse explores cases of sinkholes in Godstone, Surrey, a collapse under a main road in Yashio City in Japan and the underground quarries that are beneath ten per cent of Paris to help explain why sinkholes occur and how they can be prevented.

programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
The four chefs who have survived the intensity of the heats are back in the kitchen. Now they must prove to Marcus and Monica that they have the consistency, confidence and creativity to take on the next level of the competition.
First up is the invention test, where the chefs must put pistachio centre stage and show Marcus and Monica what they can do with it. It’s an ingredient that naturally lends itself to pastry and desserts, but used cleverly in a savoury dish, it could give one chef the edge. Will anyone dare to take it somewhere unexpected?
But the chefs aren’t finished yet. Their next test takes them out of the kitchen and into the company of three of the country’s most influential food critics: William Sitwell, Jimi Famurewa and, taking her place alongside them for the first time, Ixta Belfrage, a recipe developer and cookbook author who spent five years working at the Ottolenghi Test Kitchen.
The chefs must cook a two-course menu that showcases their food, ideas and technical ability, knowing that every element will be scrutinised by some of the toughest palates in the business. This is their chance to prove they can produce food that excites and surprises. However, impressing three professional critics is no easy feat, and their verdicts could have a major bearing on what happens next.
Back in the kitchen, Marcus and Monica must weigh up everything they have seen and tasted before deciding which chefs have done enough to progress. With only three places in knockout week available, one mistake, an underwhelming plate or a missed opportunity could make all the difference. Who will earn their place in the next stage – and whose journey ends here?
The pressure is mounting as the chefs edge closer to the coveted MasterChef: The Professionals title. Judge - Marcus Wareing Judge - Monica Galetti Series Editor - Antonia Lloyd Series Director - Emma Reynolds Executive Producer - Kelly Sparks Production Company - Shine TV.

programme.title: Escaping Idi Amin
programme.desc:
In August 1972, Idi Amin is 18 months into his dictatorship. Supporters hail the new president - a former boxer and soldier - as a saviour, and his rise to power is greeted with celebration and hope across Uganda.
But beneath the apparent social harmony, resentment runs deep. Until 1962, Uganda had been a protectorate of the British - with the British very much at the top of the pile, Africans at the bottom and Asians in the middle. Despite ten years of independence, many Africans feel that they are denied opportunities to improve their position in society. Idi Amin decides to exploit their feelings and increase support for his regime.
With one announcement from the president, the lives of 80,000 people in Uganda are changed forever. In a bid to cement his leadership, Idi Amin announces that all Ugandan Asians must leave the country within 90 days. Will they be able to flee on their British passports? programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
Michael’s journey along the coast of Northumberland continues towards the Farne Islands, takes in the holy island of Lindisfarne, and finishes in England’s northernmost town, Berwick-upon-Tweed.
On the largest of the Farne Islands, Inner Farne, Michael pitches in to help rangers clear a toxic plant which is invading the island. It’s so prolific that it’s threatening the native plants upon which seabirds depend for nesting.
From the mainland, Michael sets off on a two-mile pilgrimage along a single-track causeway, which twice a day is covered by the North Sea. His destination is the holy island of Lindisfarne. Michael discovers that the island was chosen in the seventh century by St Aidan as the site for a monastery. Northumbria’s patron saint, St Cuthbert, later became bishop there. The vicar of the island today shows Michael a full-sized reproduction of the beautifully illuminated Lindisfarne Gospels, the originals of which are held in the British Museum.
Back on the East Coast Main Line, Michael hugs the North Sea coast, crossing the River Tweed on Robert Stephenson’s Royal Border Bridge to reach Britain’s most northern town, Berwick-upon-Tweed. Struck by the variety of accents and dialects in the north east, Michael learns what distinguishes a Geordie from a Smoggie.

Michael begs permission from the town’s mayor to join horses and riders in a ceremony to mark the border between Scotland and England along a line agreed in 1438. programme.title: Sunday Morning Live
programme.desc: Sean Fletcher and Holly Hamilton host a pre-recorded, end of year episode of the show that puts the heart and soul into Sundays, bringing faith and ethics to the discussions that matter most. We reflect on a year when warnings of the risks facing humanity have regularly been in the news, and examine the impact these themes could have on society as we ask; Can a crisis bring us together? And, a year after Dame Sarah Mullaly was formally elected as Archbishop of Canterbury, we discuss what the future of the church could look like. Plus, we hear the story of the Scottish teenager who could become a saint.

programme.title: Celebration Kitchen
programme.desc:
Matt Tebbutt hosts this special edition celebrating Guru Nanak Gurpurab or the Birthday of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. Considered one of the most important Sikh holy days, it is a revered celebration in Sikhism which brings people together in devotion, reflection and unity.
Every year, the occasion is marked on the full moon day of the Kartik month, which is also known as Kartik Purnima, and falls on Tuesday 24 November this year. Three exceptional cooks join Matt in the studio to share their delicious recipes that are perfect for the celebration. Award-winning British Indian food writer, columnist and trend consultant Gurdeep Loyal prepares extra-crispy potato and chickpea tikkis with a tamarind and date chutney, which would traditionally be served as street food outside the temple. Food writer, restaurateur and chef-owner of Jikoni, Ravinder Bhogal, prepares a decadent, celebratory vegetarian platter, and as no feast is complete without a sweet treat, Manpreet Singh Ahuja, aka the Singing Chef, serves up a trio of delicious sweets, including the pinnis that he remembers his mother and grandmother making for Guru Nanak Ji's birthday.
Celebrity guests include doctor and BAFTA award-winning TV presenter Dr Ranj Singh, journalist, broadcaster and best-selling author Sathnam Sanghera and journalist, broadcaster and Good Morning Britain host Ranvir Singh, who shares her cherished Guru Nanak Gurpurab traditions, memories and food favourites from the celebration. The programme also features highlights from the BBC archives. It is a show filled with fun, food and fascinating insights into one of the most important days in the Sikh calendar. Presenter - Matt Tebbutt Executive Producer - Amanda Ross Series Producer - Pollyanne Conway Series Producer - James Bedwell Production Company - Cactus TV.

programme.title: Bargain Hunt
programme.desc:
From the Golden Globes to the Emmys, it’s awards season on the show as Natasha Raskin Sharp marvels at movie memorabilia, all owned by a familiar face – Bargain Hunt expert and film fan Stephanie Connell.
Steph shares with Natasha items from her own collection, including awards given to Sir John Gielgud and an original prop from 1970 film Julius Caesar, starring Charlton Heston.
In a Brackley antiques centre, two teams hope to find some blockbuster buys of their own, helped by leading men Tim Weeks and Thomas Forrester.
And in the grand finale at the auction in Derbyshire, auctioneer James Lewis gives his verdict on the teams’ items. programme.title: Songs of Praise
programme.desc:
Sean Fletcher is in Liverpool to meet celebrated screenwriter, author and former Children’s Laureate Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who chooses his favourite hymns and reflects on life, faith and the value of wonder.
Sean meets Frank at Liverpool’s historic waterfront, where Frank's story began, and discovers how a childhood steeped in Catholic community and the stories of saints inspired his young imagination.
In Liverpool’s Central Library, Sean hears how Frank went on to become a screenwriter for TV and film, and a best-selling children’s author. He also reveals how he came to write the narrative for the iconic opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics and why the concept of wonder has always been crucial to his work and faith.
Their journey through Liverpool finally brings them to the city’s iconic Metropolitan Cathedral, where Frank talks of the architecture as a prayer and tells of hearing his children sing there many years ago.
With hymns and songs from across the UK, chosen specially by Frank to mark the important milestones along his faith journey:
Tell Out My Soul - Huddersfield Town HallI, The Lord of Sea and Sky - Salisbury CathedralMake Me a Channel of Your Peace - St Cuthbert’s Chapel, Ushaw Historic HouseAbide with Me - The Birkenhead PrioryLove Divine – Abigail, Young Chorister of the Year semi-finalist 2022Hail Redeemer King Divine - Southwark Cathedral Presenter - Sean Fletcher Producer - Becci Dyson Series Producer - David Waters Executive Producer - Caroline Matthews Executive Producer - Paula Trafford Production Company - CTVC.

He soon becomes embroiled in a madcap plan to enter a national Song for Christmas competition and finds himself embarking on a disastrous road trip in search of the competition venue - the Christmas Castle. Lost in the wilderness with a class of small children, a baby and a donkey, he has to stand up, face his fears and try to lead them not only to safety, but victory. programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The oceans have seasons just as the land does. Stretching across the temperate bands located between the freezing poles and the warm tropics lie the seasonal seas. Life is tough in these constantly changing waters, but if animals can persevere and adapt to change, there are myriad opportunities to not only survive but thrive here.
Winter in the seasonal seas is a battlefield. Storms whip up immense waves that can travel for thousands of miles, building to 30 metres in height before making landfall. On the Pacific coast of South America, such waves impact the lives of South America sea lions that have lived on this exposed coast for generations. Newborn pups and mothers are restricted to the colony, but the most intrepid males take a risk, leaving the tempestuous coast for unfamiliar waters and unusual prey - black-necked swans.
Some choose to escape, whilst others are undeterred by winters icy grip on the seasonal seas. In Patagonia, a female southern right whale arrives in the protected bay where she was likely born, in search of a mate. Testing prospective partners before accepting the best mate, she is rewarded with a gentle belly rub and embrace - a valuable pairing given that these animals were hunted to near extinction in the last century. The whaling ban increased this population from just 300 to 25,000, with a surprising twist – white calves.
As daylight lengthens and spring approaches, the greening of the seasonal seas commences. Plankton multiplies, creating huge blooms and feeding many species, including a rather peculiar crustacean, a porcelain crab. In the waters off Chile, over 200 million feast on this bounty, forming the largest-known aggregation of crabs in our oceans. But with limited space and an increased flow of plankton, the crabs do something remarkable - they organise themselves into structured lines, a behaviour that has never been filmed before.
As forests flourish on land, they also do so in the water. In spring, kelp, one of the fastest-growing organisms on earth, can lengthen by half a metre a day, forming submarine jungles that are home to a variety of creatures. In Japan, these lush fronds conceal a rarely seen fish, an eelpout, with a length of just ten centimetres.

programme.title: Countryfile
programme.desc:
Charlotte Smith and Sean Fletcher are in the Ceiriog Valley in north Wales, meeting former clinical vet Claire Whittle, who took on an upland farm two years ago. Charlotte finds out why Claire made the leap into farming and what regenerative farming means to her, before helping with health and pregnancy checks on her cattle.
Sean gets stuck into a cow pat to explore the hidden world of dung beetles and helps plant trees in a new agroforestry field. Meanwhile, Tom investigates changes that could be coming for the game bird shooting industry. Presenter - Sean Fletcher Presenter - Tom Heap Presenter - Charlotte Smith Series Editor - Mark Beech Series Producer - Becky Pratt.

programme.title: Antiques Roadshow
programme.desc:
The roadshow comes from Alexandra Gardens in the heart of Cardiff, where treasures include a Maori pipe, a book listing wartime spies and a rare SAS medal collection.
Ronnie Archer-Morgan is thrilled to see a pipe by a renowned Maori craftsman, whilst Geoffrey Munn is dazzled by a jewel-encrusted stick pin given as a gift from King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra.
There are plenty of Welsh treasures to be found, including an autograph book featuring a Tom Jones signature and early concert ticket, and Lisa Lloyd challenges Fiona to spot the most valuable item in a group of three pieces of rare rugby memorabilia.
Marc Allum is stunned to see a remarkable archive of First World War-era photographs documenting arrivals into Cardiff Docks, some of whom were suspected of being spies, and militaria expert Mark Smith is humbled by a group of medals and a cap badge belonging to one of the earliest members of the SAS.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
In the frozen waters of the Arctic, a bowhead whale breaks the sea ice with its skull to breathe - completely at home in this seemingly hostile sea. Polar waters may seem remote, but their influence supports more than the wildlife that thrives there by helping to power a global system of ocean currents that creates extraordinary opportunities for wildlife far beyond the ice.
In the Falkland Islands, nutrient-rich water flowing north from Antarctica sustains a colony of king penguins. But returning parents weighed down with food for their chicks must try to cross a beach patrolled by an extraordinary southern sea lion, the only one known to regularly hunt king penguins on land.
Cold water from the Arctic also travels thousands of miles. In the Pacific, it cools the coast of Japan, where a male dwarf lumpsucker, about the size of a pea, must find a nest and persuade a female to enter. Once she has laid her eggs, he becomes a devoted single father, guarding them from hungry predators for 40 days and nights.
Around Antarctica, hundreds of fin whales converge on one of the greatest feeding grounds on earth. They work together in a spectacular synchronised formation, turning clockwise before lunging onto their sides to feast on Antarctic krill. Beneath the continent’s sea ice lies a remarkable world where giant sea spiders clamber over ancient glass sponges and a tiny amphipod escapes hungry icefish by hitching a ride on sea angels and venomous jellyfish.
The influence of the polar waters is so strong that it helps power global currents that cross entire oceans and circle the planet. In the North Atlantic, the Gulf Stream brings warm water from the Caribbean to the shores of Britain, attracting Atlantic bluefin tuna to hunt off the Cornish coast. These powerful predators, which can attack at 45 miles per hour, have only recently returned to British shores following international action to protect them.
But the currents all these animals rely on are changing. With a loss of sea ice, many are now weakening, driving animals to adapt – sometimes in surprising ways. Around Newfoundland, green sea urchins are losing the kelp forests that once protected them from the sun’s ultraviolet rays.

programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Glasgow - A Fix at the Top of the Cathedral ║ S1
programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Dom and Lucia are in Scotland’s biggest city for one of their biggest, or at least highest, fixes yet. Roof works mean once-in-a-generation access to Glasgow Cathedral’s weathervane, so the pair are helping blacksmith Stacey and apprentice Jameel clean and re-gild this iconic cockerel. The medieval building has a storied history, but it definitely predates lifts, so Lucia volunteers to go boldly where no Repair Shop expert has gone before – straight to the top of the 225-foot-high spire.
Back on solid ground, Kaming, a member of Glasgow’s Hakka Chinese community, has a Chinese unicorn head he hopes Lucia can bring back to life. The fragile bamboo-and-paper mask plays an important part in celebrations and festivities, but years of vigorous dancing have left it tattered and torn, its once-proud horn now held on with sticky tape. As he is the last person, as far as he is aware, who still knows how to do the traditional dance associated with the mask, he hopes having the costume repaired will mean he’s able to teach it to future generations before it's lost forever. It’s not a simple fix though, as Lucia has to contend with unfamiliar materials and balance her artistic restoration with creating a mask that will stand up structurally to years' more use in the future.
As they travel the country, the Repair Shop experts love to meet fellow craftspeople, but it’s not all stonemasonry and pottery. There’s been a vibrant graffiti scene in Glasgow for decades, and Dom is meeting celebrated street artist Pizzaboy to discover how his large-scale works engage with the local community. programme.desc:
Five chefs remain in the race for a spot in the quarter-final, but first they must impress in two more challenges designed to test their creativity, precision and technical ability.
Marcus and Monica are joined by acclaimed South African chef Ash Valenzuela-Heeger, winner of the prestigious 2025 Michelin Young Chef Award. Her impressive career has seen her hone her craft at some of the world’s most celebrated restaurants, including London’s three-Michelin-starred Ledbury and Cape Town’s renowned Test Kitchen. She has since made her mark with Riverine Rabbit in Birmingham, which earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand in 2025.
Known for her bold, inventive cooking, Ash draws on her South African heritage and international influences, with live-fire techniques at the heart of her culinary style. She challenges the chefs to cook BBQ beef sirloin, served with BBQ maitake mushrooms, caramelised roscoff onions and a cafe au lait sauce. It’s a brief that demands a sophisticated understanding of flavour, smoke and fire, and the ability to make every element work in harmony.
With the standard rising and a quarter-final place within reach, can the contestants deliver a plate worthy of this award-winning chef’s exacting standards?
The signature dessert round is the final hurdle, and the chefs must show that they have the range and imagination to compete with the very best. This is their chance to take risks, bring their own ideas to the plate and prove that they can deliver something truly memorable. But sweet cooking demands a different kind of judgement; flavours must work in harmony, textures need to complement one another, and the finishing touches can make all the difference between a good dessert and a great one.
Marcus and Monica have seen what the chefs can do with savoury ingredients, but now they must decide who has the finesse and creative flair to progress to the next stage of the competition. As the final plates are tasted, will the desserts be enough to secure a place in the quarter-final? And whose MasterChef journey must come to an end? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
It’s the last quarter-final of the series, and with a place in knockout week at stake, there’s everything to play for. Four chefs return to the kitchen knowing that one false move could bring their ambitions to an abrupt end. Marcus and Monica are looking for the consistency, ingenuity and confidence that mark out a truly exceptional chef.
First up is the invention test, and the secret ingredient has a history stretching back more than 2,000 years: miso. A staple of Japanese cuisine, this fermented paste brings extraordinary depth, savoury complexity and umami to a dish. With different varieties offering their own distinctive flavours, the chefs must work out how best to make miso the star of the plate. Who will turn this humble ingredient into something exceptional, and who will fall short of expectations?
Then they face one last chance to prove they have what it takes to go all the way.
Three highly respected food writers and critics, Tom Parker Bowles, Leyla Kazim and Jimi Famurewa, wait to put the chefs’ cooking under the microscope. They know what exceptional food looks, tastes and feels like, and they’ll be looking beyond technical skill to the details that separate a good meal from a truly memorable one.
The chefs must serve up a two-course menu that captures their culinary identity, showcases their abilities and gives these exacting critics something to talk about. Every choice matters, from the balance of flavours to the smallest finishing touch. Can they cook with enough originality and precision to make a lasting impression?
Back in the kitchen, Marcus and Monica face their biggest decision yet. With the quarter-finals coming to a close and only three places in knockout week up for grabs, they must consider the chefs’ performances across the challenges before deciding who has done enough to progress to the next stage. Who will take the next step towards the coveted MasterChef: The Professionals title, and whose journey ends at the final hurdle?

When a burnt-out delivery van is discovered on a quiet rural road, Rose and Raj are met with a grim crime scene: a charred body in the passenger seat and no sign of the driver. Sifting through the ashes, they uncover a bizarre assortment of clues, including a melted key fob, rusted gardening tools and a bottle of imported Polish vodka.
Tracking down the van’s insured drivers leads them to Kelly Prudham, a tight-lipped agency cleaner, and Scott Smith, a devoted widowed father missing since the previous evening. Is Scott the vanished driver, or is he the unidentified victim in the passenger seat? Kelly claims concern for Scott’s young daughter Chloe, yet she stonewalls every question. However, Rose’s sharp eyes spot an identical bottle of Polish vodka in Kelly’s flat, indicating that Kelly may have a dangerous motive for concealing her and Scott’s recent movements.
Meanwhile, Joe can’t resist probing into the mystery. Dragging Brother Christopher along, he snoops around the crime scene and dives into Scott’s past. Relying on his sharp human intuition and feeling somewhat aligned with this man who seems to be struggling as a father, Joe forms a bold theory about Scott’s whereabouts. But his covert search goes sideways, stranding Joe and Christopher in a perilous predicament deep in the Northumbrian moors.
With time running out and danger escalating, Rose, Joe and Raj must pool their findings to identify the burnt remains, track down the arsonist and expose the motive behind the blaze before the truth burns out completely. Will and Kirsten are in Musselburgh, on Scotland’s east coast. It’s a town boasting a proud heritage that is celebrated each year with a procession led by their elected Honest Lad and Honest Lass. Restoring the carriage is a huge job that requires the skills of local signwriter Ross Hastie and wheelwright Greg Rowland, and made more complicated by the impending deadline of this year’s festival.
It's a bit of a musical mystery when the team are faced with Erica’s Stroviol. In the family since the 1930s, it belonged to Erica's father, who was a passionate musician who played in several local groups. The distinctive horn has become detached from this turn-of-the-century musical oddity, so it might take more than just the skills of stringed instrument expert Becky Houghton to get a tune out of it once again.
In nearby Edinburgh, Will stops off at Stewart Christie & Co, Scotland’s oldest bespoke tailors, to discover how their handmade tweed clothes balance modern demands with century-old techniques. Will gets an insight into every step of the process, from an initial measuring to getting on the scissors himself and cutting out his own waistcoat pattern from the tweed cloth the company built their name on. programme.title: Policing Paradise
programme.desc:
With exclusive access to the police service on the paradise island of Bermuda, we follow life on the front line for the near 400 officers keeping both holidaymakers and locals safe. From patrols and traffic operations to the drug unit, forensics, tactical response teams, the coastguard and community policing, the series goes behind the scenes with the officers at the heart of the action.
The island has its fair share of challenges on both land and sea, with more than 3,000 crimes committed each year. We show how these dedicated officers, including around 30 from the UK, deal with the highs and lows of policing this British Overseas Territory.
In the centre of the island, Sergeant Milton Hill responds to reports of an elderly man walking along a busy roadside in clear distress. When he arrives, the man is unable to recall his name, address or basic personal details, and the mystery begins. Concerned for his safety, Milton stays close, guiding traffic around him as he repeatedly steps into the road. On an island where everyone knows everyone, Officer Milton sends a photograph of the man to base, where his identity provides a surprising twist to the tale. It's a race against time for Officer Milton to get him returned home safely.
Elsewhere, PC Eddie Smith and PC Jameela Sabir are on a stop-and-search operation. When Sergeant Mervin Homer examines a bike, he discovers a dangerous switchblade hidden under the seat. With the rider offering no feasible explanation, the prohibited weapon is immediately seized. Back at Hamilton Police Station, Custody Sergeant Francis Blackman reads the bike rider their rights, while Assistant Commissioner Martin Weekes examines other recently confiscated blades, including machetes and a samurai sword.
At Bermuda’s international airport, PC Paul 'Geordie' Watson supports Customs Officer Malcolm Martin and drugs dog Zorro while screening an incoming flight from Canada. After sweeping the aircraft cabin in just five minutes, Zorro indicates interest in two bags in the arrivals hall, leaving customs officers the job of discreetly monitoring the family before searching their bags and bringing them in for questioning. What will the canine team uncover next?

programme.title: Celebration Kitchen
programme.desc:
Matt Tebbutt hosts this special edition celebrating Guru Nanak Gurpurab or the Birthday of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. Considered one of the most important Sikh holy days, it is a revered celebration in Sikhism which brings people together in devotion, reflection and unity.
Every year, the occasion is marked on the full moon day of the Kartik month, which is also known as Kartik Purnima, and falls on Tuesday 24 November this year. Three exceptional cooks join Matt in the studio to share their delicious recipes that are perfect for the celebration. Award-winning British Indian food writer, columnist and trend consultant Gurdeep Loyal prepares extra-crispy potato and chickpea tikkis with a tamarind and date chutney, which would traditionally be served as street food outside the temple. Food writer, restaurateur and chef-owner of Jikoni, Ravinder Bhogal, prepares a decadent, celebratory vegetarian platter, and as no feast is complete without a sweet treat, Manpreet Singh Ahuja, aka the Singing Chef, serves up a trio of delicious sweets, including the pinnis that he remembers his mother and grandmother making for Guru Nanak Ji's birthday.
Celebrity guests include doctor and BAFTA award-winning TV presenter Dr Ranj Singh, journalist, broadcaster and best-selling author Sathnam Sanghera and journalist, broadcaster and Good Morning Britain host Ranvir Singh, who shares her cherished Guru Nanak Gurpurab traditions, memories and food favourites from the celebration. The programme also features highlights from the BBC archives. It is a show filled with fun, food and fascinating insights into one of the most important days in the Sikh calendar. programme.title: Songs of Praise
programme.desc:
Sean Fletcher is in Liverpool to meet celebrated screenwriter, author and former Children’s Laureate Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who chooses his favourite hymns and reflects on life, faith and the value of wonder.
Sean meets Frank at Liverpool’s historic waterfront, where Frank's story began, and discovers how a childhood steeped in Catholic community and the stories of saints inspired his young imagination.
In Liverpool’s Central Library, Sean hears how Frank went on to become a screenwriter for TV and film, and a best-selling children’s author. He also reveals how he came to write the narrative for the iconic opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics and why the concept of wonder has always been crucial to his work and faith.
Their journey through Liverpool finally brings them to the city’s iconic Metropolitan Cathedral, where Frank talks of the architecture as a prayer and tells of hearing his children sing there many years ago.
With hymns and songs from across the UK, chosen specially by Frank to mark the important milestones along his faith journey:
